subject: general
question: Which harvest festival is celebrated in Punjab during January?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Lohri**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Lohri** is a popular **harvest festival** celebrated primarily in the **Punjab** region of the Indian subcontinent. It is observed with great enthusiasm by both **Sikhs** and **Hindus** to mark the end of the peak winter season.

• The festival is celebrated every year on the **13th of January**, just a day before **Makar Sankranti**. It signifies the sun's entry into the northern hemisphere, known as **Uttarayana**, leading to longer days and shorter nights.

• It is traditionally associated with the harvest of **Rabi crops**, particularly **sugarcane**. Farmers in **Punjab** and **Haryana** offer prayers and thanks to the **Almighty** for a successful harvest and pray for prosperity in the coming season.

• The central ritual of **Lohri** is the lighting of a **bonfire** after sunset. People gather around the fire, sing traditional folk songs, and perform **Bhangra** and **Gidda**. Offerings of **til** (sesame seeds), **gajak**, **gur** (jaggery), **popcorn**, and **rewri** are thrown into the fire as a tribute to the **God of Fire (Agni)**.

• The festival is also deeply linked to the legend of **Dulla Bhatti**, a local hero who lived during the reign of **Emperor Akbar**. He is remembered for rescuing young girls from being sold into slavery and arranging their marriages. The famous folk song **Sunder Mundriye** is sung during the celebrations to honor his bravery.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Pongal**: This is a **four-day** harvest festival celebrated in the state of **Tamil Nadu**. It usually falls between **January 14th and 17th**. It is dedicated to the **Sun God (Surya)** and involves the ritual of boiling fresh rice in milk in a clay pot until it overflows, symbolizing abundance.

• **Bihu**: Specifically **Magh Bihu** (also known as **Bhogali Bihu**), is the harvest festival of **Assam** celebrated in **January**. It marks the end of the harvesting season in the month of **Maagha**. People build temporary huts called **Meji** and **Bhelaghar** from bamboo and thatch, which are burned the next morning.

• **Makar Sankranti**: This is a major pan-Indian festival that marks the transition of the **Sun** into the zodiac sign of **Capricorn (Makara)**. While it is celebrated on **January 14th or 15th**, it is known by various names such as **Uttarayan** in **Gujarat** (famous for kite flying), **Poush Sankranti** in **West Bengal**, and **Khichdi** in **Uttar Pradesh**.

• **Vaisakhi**: Although it is also a harvest festival in **Punjab**, it is celebrated in the month of **April** (usually **April 13th or 14th**). It marks the ripening of the **wheat (Rabi) crop** and also commemorates the formation of the **Khalsa Panth** by **Guru Gobind Singh** in **1699**.

**Important Points__**

• **Social Significance**: **Lohri** holds special importance for families that have recently celebrated a **wedding** or the **birth of a child**. The 'first Lohri' of a new bride or a newborn is celebrated with extra fervor and grand feasts.

• **Traditional Cuisine**: The traditional dinner served during **Lohri** consists of **Sarson da Saag** (mustard greens) and **Makki di Roti** (cornbread), which are seasonal staples in **North India**.

• **Geographical Reach**: While it is the primary festival of **Punjab**, it is also widely celebrated in **Delhi**, **Himachal Pradesh**, and **Jammu** due to the significant **Punjabi** diaspora and cultural influence in these regions.

• **Environmental Aspect**: In recent years, there has been a growing awareness to celebrate **Eco-friendly Lohri** by reducing the size of bonfires to prevent excessive air pollution, while still maintaining the cultural essence of the festival.
